newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu rivals say he isolated in Romania election.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu rivals say he isolated in Romania election.

text.p: Opponents of Romanian President Ion Iliescu said on Monday his aggressive campaign to win re-election this week showed the former communist was becoming increasingly isolated seven years after taking power.

With six days left before a decisive run-off, Iliescu has launched fierce attacks on his challenger Emil Constantinescu, suggesting he would bring back Romania's exiled king, engineer the seizure of property and break up the country.

Iliescu finished four points ahead of Constantinescu in the presidential election's first round this month. But his Party of Social Democracy (PSDR) was trounced by Constantinescu's Democratic Convention in parliamentary polls and thrown out of government for the first time since the 1989 fall of communism.
"Iliescu lacks any political support apart from the PDSR. He is isolated on Romania's political scene," Constantinescu told a news conference.
"He is behaving like a fireman threatened with unemployment who sets a fire to boast that he has put it out. There is no fire in Romania. We have real firemen if someone tries to start one."

Once-reliable allies, including a major nationalist group, a Socialist party and Romania's tenants' association, have deserted Iliescu and support his opponent. That has left the PDSR as the only major party backing his re-election.
The candidates were holding the first of several television debates on Monday after a weekend of bitter polemics.
Iliescu told a rally in Alba Iulia in central Transylvania region that electing Constantinescu would hand all power to rightists already in control of parliament and the cabinet.
He also suggested that bringing into government a party representing the 1.6 million-strong Hungarian minority could generate demands for autonomy and threaten national unity.
"Electing Mr Constantinescu given a parliamentary majority and a government built by him would mean establishing a real political dictatorship of rightist forces," he said.
"It is vital that the institution of president be held by an outspoken republican who holds dear the interests of the nation and those who live by honest work."

The president's campaign clips, broadcast since the weekend, warn voters the homes they live in and the factories where they work could be handed back to their pre-war owners if Constantinescu wins Sunday's vote.
Most newspapers, except those firmly committed to Iliescu, have denounced his campaign strategy.

"The masks of being "European', a "democrat' and an "enlightened man' have fallen away one by one to reveal old Bolshevik habits," the daily Adevarul said. "Iliescu no longer represents even the leftists. Only himself and his entourage."
Constantinescu, a geology professor with no political career in the communist era, has received the backing of former Prime Minister Petre Roman, third-place finisher in the election's opening round.
Both men say Iliescu must be voted out to enable Romania to emerge once and for all from the legacy of communism under megalomaniac dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

The new government is committed to a 200-day plan to invigorate the economy and bridge the growing gap in living standards between Romania and other ex-communist countries which have launched faster reforms, like Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
